blurb: The machine learning that quietly runs the world: decision trees, finding groups in data, and how your feeds choose what to show you.

steps.p: Lots of real-world data is a table: each row a customer or house, each column a feature like age or price. The goal: predict one column from the others.

visual.caption: Predict a house's price from its features.

steps.p: Linear models weigh each feature and add them up. Logistic regression does the same to predict yes/no outcomes, like "will this customer leave?"
A tree asks a series of yes/no questions — "more than 2 bedrooms?", "in London?" — until it reaches a prediction.
A random forest averages hundreds of trees, each trained on random slices of the data. Gradient boosting adds trees one by one, each fixing the last ones' mistakes.
For table data, boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM) often still beat deep neural networks — and train in minutes.

cards.q: For typical spreadsheet-style data, what often beats deep neural networks?
cards.why: Boosted trees. They handle mixed columns and missing values well, need less data and tuning, and remain the go-to for tables.

cards.statement: Logistic regression is used for yes/no classification, despite its name.
cards.why: True. It predicts a probability between 0 and 1 — like "72% chance this email is spam" — then you pick a cut-off.

cards.q: A random forest makes predictions by…
options: Averaging many trees trained on random slices of the data
cards.why: Averaging many varied trees. Each tree makes different mistakes; averaging cancels many of them out.

cards.title: XGBoost was used in 17 of the 29 winning solutions on the Kaggle competition site published in 2015.
cards.detail: Tianqi Chen's gradient-boosting library became the default tool for table-data competitions, according to the XGBoost paper.

cards.statement: Decision trees need all features scaled to the same range.
cards.why: False. Trees just ask "is it above this value?", so it doesn't matter whether a column is in metres or millimetres.

steps.p: Unsupervised learning looks for structure in data with no right answers attached — groups, trends, oddities.
k-means splits data into k groups: guess k centres, assign each point to the nearest, move the centres to the middle of their groups, repeat.

items: Assign each point to nearest centre

steps.analogy: Placing k ice-cream vans on a beach so everyone's close to one.

steps.p: Principal component analysis finds the few directions where data varies most, so 100 columns can be summarised by 2 or 3.
Tools like t-SNE draw high-dimensional data as a 2D map. Nearby points are similar — but distances between separate clusters mean little.
Anomaly detection flags points unlike the rest — a strange card payment, a failing machine.

cards.q: What must you choose before running k-means clustering?
options: The correct label for every point
cards.why: k. The algorithm doesn't decide how many groups exist. People try several values and compare.

options: The directions along which the data varies most
cards.why: Directions of most variation. Keeping just the top few captures most of the information with far fewer numbers.

cards.statement: In a t-SNE map, the distances between separate clusters are reliable.
cards.why: False. t-SNE keeps close neighbours close but can stretch or shrink gaps between clusters. Don't read meaning into them.

cards.title: The k-means algorithm was developed at Bell Labs in 1957 but not published until 1982.
cards.detail: Stuart Lloyd described it in an internal report about signal processing. It's still one of the most widely used algorithms in data science.

cards.q: Which is a natural use for anomaly detection?
options: Flagging unusual card payments as possible fraud
cards.why: Fraud alerts. A £2,000 purchase abroad at 3 am looks very unlike your usual pattern.

steps.p: Collaborative filtering recommends what similar users enjoyed. If you and I both loved five films, you'll probably like my sixth.
Picture a table of every user × every item, filled with ratings. Almost all of it is blank — nobody has watched everything.

visual.caption: Fill in the blanks = predict what you'd rate.

steps.p: Matrix factorisation gives every user and item a short list of numbers for hidden traits — "how much action", "how much comedy". Multiply and add them up to predict a rating.
steps.analogy: Describing both people and films on the same handful of sliders, then checking how well they match.

steps.p: With no history, there's nothing to match — the "cold start" problem. Apps ask you to pick a few favourites to get going.
Big services first pull a few hundred candidates out of millions quickly, then carefully rank those few.

cards.q: The "cold start" problem in recommendations is about…
options: New users or items with no history to learn from
cards.why: No history yet. The system has nothing to compare, so it leans on popularity or asks you questions.

cards.q: In matrix factorisation, a predicted rating comes from…
options: Combining a user's hidden-taste numbers with an item's (a dot product)
cards.why: Matching tastes. Multiply each user slider by the item's matching slider and add them up. High result = good match.

cards.q: The Netflix Prize offered $1 million for improving Netflix's rating predictions by…
cards.why: 10%. It took teams about three years; the winners combined hundreds of models.

cards.statement: Netflix never put the full winning Netflix Prize solution into use.
cards.why: True. Netflix said the extra accuracy wasn't worth the engineering cost — and its business had shifted to streaming.

cards.title: Matrix factorisation became famous during the Netflix Prize.
cards.detail: Simon Funk described a simple version in a 2006 blog post. It quickly became a core technique of the competition and of recommendation systems generally.

cards.title: What your feed is trying to do

steps.p: Feeds rank posts by predicted chance you'll watch, like, comment or share. The highest predictions go to the top.
You watch what's shown; that becomes the data for what's shown next. Small preferences can snowball into a narrow feed.
What grabs you now isn't always what you'd choose on reflection. Optimise only for watch time and you reward compulsive content.
steps.analogy: A shop that only stocks what people grab at the till — sweets win, vegetables vanish.

steps.p: "When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure." Watch time was a hint of value; chased hard, it drifts away from it.
Feeds mix in some items they're unsure about, to learn more about you and avoid trapping you in a bubble.

cards.q: Why can optimising purely for watch time backfire?
options: It rewards compulsive content over content people value
cards.why: Measure ≠ goal. Hours watched is a stand-in for value. Push hard on it and the feed finds ways to hold attention that people don't actually want.

cards.statement: A recommender trained on clicks learns what users value in the long run.
cards.why: False. Clicks capture split-second impulses. Some services add surveys and long-term signals to get closer to what people value.

cards.q: Why do feeds deliberately show some items they're unsure about?
options: To learn more about your tastes and avoid a narrow bubble
cards.why: Exploration. Without it, the feed only ever confirms what it already thinks you like.

cards.title: TikTok said in 2020 that watching a long video to the end is a strong signal for its recommendations.
cards.detail: Its public explanation listed interactions, video information and device settings as factors, with finishing videos among the strongest.

cards.title: Train your feeds on purpose
cards.body: Every pause and replay is a vote. Use "not interested" and follow things you'd like more of, so the feed learns what you value.
cards.challenge: Spend 5 minutes today tapping "not interested" on content you regret watching, and follow two accounts that teach you something.
